summary: Finding where a fault occurs is a key operations capability for transport networks. This informational document gives requirements for monitoring a segment of an MPLS path on demand and without disturbing the traffic being carried, which existing methods cannot do well.

eli5.summary: It is like checking one stretch of a road for problems without stopping the cars that are driving on it.

questions: how to monitor part of an mpls path
how to localize mpls network faults
subtitle: On-demand monitoring of MPLS path segments without traffic disruption.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to pinpoint faults on MPLS paths, but the existing segment monitoring method (Sub-Path Maintenance Elements) requires adding layers to the network, changes path conditions, and disrupts traffic when set up on demand.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8256 specifies requirements for Hitless Path Segment Monitoring (HPSM), a new OAM function that allows monitoring arbitrary segments of MPLS paths without modifying the path or affecting traffic flow.
tldr.outcome: Operators can diagnose faults faster by monitoring individual path segments with minimal network complexity and no service disruption.

today: RFC 8256 is an Informational standard specifying requirements for HPSM. It provides a foundation for standardizing hitless path segment monitoring tools that would improve fault localization in MPLS Transport Profile networks.

sections.title: The Need for Segment Monitoring
sections.content:
When a service fails on an MPLS network, operations staff need to locate the fault quickly. End-to-end monitoring alone is insufficient because it shows only whether the entire path is working, not which segment has a problem.

RFC 8256 addresses the limitations of the current segment monitoring method defined for MPLS-TP (MPLS Transport Profile), which uses Sub-Path Maintenance Elements (SPME). While SPME can monitor segments, it introduces significant operational challenges. The RFC specifies requirements for Hitless Path Segment Monitoring (HPSM), a new monitoring capability that locates faults without network complexity or service disruption.
sections.eli5: When a network is broken, you need to find which part broke. This document explains how to test one part of the network without breaking the traffic flowing through it.

sections.title: Problems with the Current Approach
sections.content:
SPME creates a hierarchical overlay by adding additional labels to MPLS packets. This solves the problem of segment monitoring but introduces three major drawbacks.

First, SPME adds management complexity because operators must configure and maintain additional sublayers with new endpoints and intermediate points. This expands management systems significantly.

Second, SPME changes the original path conditions. Adding labels changes the exposed label values and packet length. Performance measurements like delay and packet loss become unreliable because the monitored path is no longer identical to the original path. A fault in label handling on the original LSP might be masked.

Third, on-demand SPME configuration disrupts traffic because it requires label stacking and potentially packet length changes. While a make-before-break procedure exists, it requires control-plane support and may fail when bandwidth is constrained.
sections.eli5: The current method wraps extra layers around the data, which makes the system harder to manage, changes what is being measured, and temporarily stops traffic when you turn it on.

sections.title: HPSM Functional Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 8256 defines mandatory requirements (M) and optional ones (O) for HPSM. The core mandatory requirements are that HPSM must not change the original path conditions (no label modification, no packet size change), and it must support on-demand activation without traffic disruption.

HPSM must support monitoring multiple segments simultaneously along a transport path. It must work at single or multiple nesting levels, allowing both simple single-level diagnostics and more advanced multi-level analysis. Critically, HPSM must operate independently of end-to-end proactive monitoring, so both can run concurrently without interference.

HPSM must support provisioning on arbitrary segments of a transport path. This allows operators to use a diagnostic procedure that progressively narrows down fault locations by monitoring increasingly specific segments. The granularity can be at node or interface level depending on equipment capability.
sections.eli5: HPSM can test any piece of the path without touching it, test multiple pieces at once, and work at the same time as other monitoring without getting in the way.

sections.title: Handling Failures and Management Complexity
sections.content:
When a node or link fails while HPSM is active on a protected LSP, the path may switch to a protection route with a different hop count. This could cause HPSM to terminate at an unintended node. HPSM should detect such situations and avoid monitoring the wrong segment, either by suspending monitoring or by comparing node identifiers.

A key design requirement is that HPSM should not be based on additional transport layers like hierarchical LSPs. Instead, it should reuse the same identifiers (MEPs and MIPs) already used in the network. This minimizes the number of managed objects and keeps management systems simple while providing the same diagnostic capability.
sections.eli5: If the network breaks and reroutes while monitoring is happening, HPSM should notice and stop, so it is not fooled. And the system should not add more layers to manage.

sections.title: Standards Alignment and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
HPSM is defined as an additional OAM tool, not a replacement for SPME. It must be compatible with existing SPME usage and applicable at the SPME layer itself if needed. This ensures that networks already using SPME can adopt HPSM incrementally without obsoleting their investment.

RFC 8256 specifies that HPSM must support both the per-node and per-interface OAM models already defined in RFC 6371, the MPLS-TP OAM framework. Optional requirements allow HPSM to support advanced capabilities like multi-level monitoring, providing a path for more sophisticated implementations while keeping basic implementations simple.
sections.eli5: HPSM works alongside the old monitoring method, not instead of it. It supports the same operating models the old method uses, so everyone can upgrade gradually.
